source.version: arXiv:2510.26490v1 [cs.HC], 30 Oct 2025, as printed on PDF p. 1.
source.title_on_document: SCAFFOLDING CREATIVITY: HOW DIVERGENT AND CONVERGENT LLM PERSONAS SHAPE HUMAN MACHINE CREATIVE PROBLEM-SOLVING

supplement.holds: No supplement or online appendix is referenced. The PDF ends with references and contains no appendix; output statistics are in section 5.3 and Figure 6 (pp. 9–10).

paper_design_summary: Undergraduates were individually randomized to a chat interface offering switchable divergent and convergent LLM personas or to the same interface with standard ChatGPT behind both buttons; both groups used AI to generate ideas for making libraries more attractive to young adults (p. 4, section 4). The paper reports 105 randomized and 101 analyzed, although the analyzed arm counts conflict between the text and Figure 6 (pp. 4–5, sections 4–5; p. 10, Figure 6). Ideas extracted from user transcripts were scored for fluency, semantic separation across participants, and semantic variation within each participant's portfolio, all from the AI-assisted session (pp. 9–10, section 5.3).

studies.label: Randomized persona-guided versus standard ChatGPT library-ideation experiment; setting not stated

assignment.what_was_assigned: Individuals were assigned to the persona-guided interface or the baseline ChatGPT interface. Treatment participants could use both Taylor and Alex; divergent and convergent personas were not separate randomized arms. The between-condition manipulation is explicit, but the PDF does not specify laboratory supervision, online-panel delivery, or ordinary-work/coursework delivery sufficiently to select lab_rct, online_rct, or field_rct (p. 4, section 4; p. 11, section 6).
assignment.quote: Random assignment allocated 73 participants to the treatment group and 32 to the control group.
assignment.prereg_locator: No preregistration statement or registry link in the PDF.

arms.name: Persona-guided ChatGPT (Taylor and Alex)
arms.description: Both personas were available within the same chat: Taylor used divergent-thinking prompts and temperature 0.8, while Alex used convergent-thinking prompts and temperature 0.3 (p. 4, section 4). The analyzed count here follows the results text; Figure 6 instead labels treatment n=70 (p. 5, section 5; p. 10, Figure 6).

arms.name: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
arms.description: Both buttons routed to the same baseline ChatGPT model with unmodified responses (p. 4, section 4). The analyzed count here follows the results text; Figure 6 instead labels control n=31 (p. 5, section 5; p. 10, Figure 6).

participants.exclusions: The paper states that four of 105 participants were excluded, but lists minimal interaction (n=1), inadequate session duration (n=2), session timeout violations (n=1), and content authenticity issues (n=1); whether reasons overlap is not explained. The results text gives 101 conversation logs, 69 treatment and 32 control. Figure 6 instead labels the analyzed arms n=70 and n=31. An additional three participants per group were excluded only from survey analysis for incomplete questionnaires; these survey exclusions are not applied to the conversation-output sample (pp. 5–6, section 5; p. 10, Figure 6).
participants.who: Undergraduate students from a design and engineering institution; the participant institution is not named (p. 4, section 4).
participants.quote: The final dataset comprised 101 conversation logs: 69 from the persona condition and 32 from the control condition.
participants.locator: p. 4, section 4 (people randomized); pp. 5–6, section 5 (analyzed sample and exclusions); p. 10, Figure 6 (conflicting arm counts)

ai_tool.name_model: ChatGPT; the experimental chat model version is not stated. GPT-4.1 is named only for post hoc idea extraction, and text-embedding-3-large for scoring (p. 4, section 4; p. 9, section 5.3).
ai_tool.how_used: Participants freely switched between two chat buttons. Treatment prompts differentiated divergent and convergent behavior; control buttons both used unmodified baseline ChatGPT. A static system prompt, JSON conversation-state summary, and recent transcript maintained context. Although the authors call the interface coach-like, it also supplies content, as shown in Figure 1, so it does not meet the codebook's content-free coach definition (pp. 4–5, section 4 and Figure 1; p. 11, section 6).

task.description: Generate ideas addressing: How can we make libraries more attractive to young adults? Ideas were extracted from the user transcripts of the human–LLM interaction (p. 4, section 4; p. 9, section 5.3).
task.duration: 20-minute task following a five-minute interface orientation (p. 4, section 4).

outcomes.name: Between-participant semantic differentiation (paper: participant-level originality)
outcomes.question: across_people
outcomes.measure_detail: GPT-4.1 extracted ideas from user transcripts. Each participant's portfolio was represented by the mean-pooled centroid of normalized OpenAI text-embedding-3-large idea embeddings. The primary variant was mean cosine distance to same-condition peers, explicitly marked primary in Figure 6. The all-participant mean-distance and nearest cross-condition neighbor-distance variants are kept in this outcome rather than counted as separate outcomes. These measures compare different participants' portfolios and therefore use the codebook's diversity construct despite the paper's originality label (pp. 9–10, section 5.3; p. 10, Figure 6).

contrasts.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
contrasts.reported: Same-condition originality: Treatment M=0.34, Control M=0.28; Welch’s t, p=2.20 × 10−6 (text). Figure 6 prints Welch p = 2.2e-06. All-participant originality: Treatment M=0.33, Control M=0.31; p=.02 (text); Figure 6 prints Welch p = 0.0215. Cross-condition nearest neighbor distance: Treatment M=0.20, Control M=0.17; p<.01 (text); Figure 6 prints Welch p = 0.00249. Figure 6 labels all three comparisons treatment n=70, control n=31, conflicting with the 69/32 analyzed split on p. 5. No numerical SD, SE, t statistic, degrees of freedom, or confidence-interval endpoints are reported for these contrasts.
contrasts.locator: pp. 9–10, section 5.3, Computational Creativity Assessment; p. 10, Figure 6, including its image labels; p. 5, section 5 for the conflicting counts

diversity_detail.metric: Cosine distance between participant-level portfolio centroids; larger values mean greater semantic separation. The same-condition mean-distance variant is primary.
diversity_detail.computed_over: For each participant, the mean distance to same-condition peers; variants use mean distance to all participants and the nearest cross-condition neighbor. The analyzed score belongs to the participant, not to an individual idea pair (pp. 9–10, section 5.3; p. 10, Figure 6).
diversity_detail.uncertainty: Welch tests compare participant-level distance scores; Figure 6 reports Welch p values for all three variants. Error bars are drawn, but their type and numerical endpoints are not defined in the text or caption. No adjustment for dependence induced by shared comparison portfolios is described (p. 10, section 5.3 and Figure 6).
diversity_detail.notes: The paper calls these originality measures and refers to human–LLM teams, but the analysis is explicitly participant-level. No sign reversal is needed because the reported metric is distance. The arm-count conflict prevents treating either arm split as unambiguous for these estimates. The statistics_available code p_value_only describes the reported inferential information; rounded arm means are also printed.

outcomes.name: Idea fluency
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Number of ideas per participant, using a two-stage content-analysis pipeline: GPT-4.1 structured extraction from user transcripts followed by category induction. This is a count of ideas, not a count of participants; the condition comparison is participant-level (p. 9, section 5.3).

contrasts.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
contrasts.reported: Treatment M=8.55, SD=3.85; Control M=9.23, SD=3.37. The text states no significant between-condition differences but gives no exact p value or test statistic. No fluency-specific arm counts are printed; the overall results sample is reported as 69 treatment and 32 control on p. 5, with a conflicting 70/31 split shown for originality in Figure 6.
contrasts.locator: p. 9, section 5.3, Computational Creativity Assessment (means, SDs, and direction); p. 5, section 5 (overall analysis counts); p. 10, Figure 6 (conflicting originality counts)

outcomes.name: Within-participant idea-portfolio variation
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Mean pairwise semantic distance among the ideas within each participant's own portfolio, reported as within-participant idea diversity. The semantic analysis uses OpenAI text-embedding-3-large. Coded flexibility because this measures variation within a person's ideas, not diversity across different people (pp. 9–10, section 5.3).

contrasts.control_arm: Standard ChatGPT (identical baseline behind both buttons)
contrasts.reported: Mean pairwise distance: Treatment M=0.59, Control M=0.59, p=.90. No numerical SD, SE, test statistic, confidence interval, or outcome-specific sample counts are printed.
contrasts.locator: p. 10, section 5.3, paragraph beginning Within-participant idea diversity

company_involvement.description: No company funding, company-author affiliation, or company role in conducting the study is disclosed. Use of ChatGPT and OpenAI analysis tools is reported, but does not establish company participation.
company_involvement.locator: p. 1, author affiliations; p. 4, section 4; p. 9, section 5.3; no company-involvement disclosure elsewhere in the PDF.

eligibility.reason: Random assignment of individuals to two generative-AI configurations is explicit (p. 4, section 4), which qualifies as ai_design even though there is no no-AI arm. The paper reports 101 analyzed participants, exceeding 50; the text and Figure 6 disagree on the arm split but give the same combined sample size (p. 5, section 5; p. 10, Figure 6). Fluency and semantic-distance measures are computed from participants' generated ideas (pp. 9–10, section 5.3). All scored output was produced during AI interaction; no unassisted post-AI creative task is reported (pp. 4–5, section 4; p. 9, section 5.3). The exact RCT setting is unresolved, so design_class is other rather than an unsupported lab/online/field subtype; this does not change the three explicit eligibility criteria.

one_line_finding: Persona-guided ChatGPT increased between-participant semantic distance relative to standard ChatGPT (M=0.34 vs 0.28; p=2.20 × 10−6), with no significant difference in idea fluency or within-person variation (pp. 9–10, section 5.3; p. 10, Figure 6).
open_questions: Which analyzed arm counts are correct: 69 treatment/32 control in the results text (p. 5, section 5), or 70/31 printed on every comparison in Figure 6 (p. 10)? Confirm outcome-specific counts before effect extraction.
The text states four exclusions but lists reason counts of 1, 2, 1, and 1 (p. 5, section 5). Did reasons overlap, or is an exclusion count incorrect?

Was the randomized session supervised in a laboratory, conducted remotely, or embedded in ordinary coursework? The setting needed to choose lab_rct, online_rct, or field_rct is not stated in section 4 (pp. 4–5).
What do the Figure 6 error bars represent? Numerical uncertainty estimates and their definition are not supplied (p. 10, Figure 6 and caption).
Which ChatGPT model/version generated the experimental chat responses? Section 4 does not identify it; GPT-4.1 is specified only for subsequent idea extraction (p. 4, section 4; p. 9, section 5.3).
notes: Screened the entire markdown from start to finish, including references; the PDF has no appended supplement. PDF text was checked for the source version, design, assignment, counts, exclusions, methods, and all recorded output statistics. Figure 1 and Figure 6 were also inspected as images in memory. No effect sizes were computed. The three between-participant distance variants are retained together as one outcome under the form's variant rule. Self-reported creativity, persona preferences, ownership, personality associations, and question-asking process measures are excluded from the output-outcome list. Section 5.3 discusses elaboration and category-based flexibility conceptually but does not report separate scored comparisons for them. No shared sample with another paper, preregistration, or data/code URL is stated. Country is left not_stated because author affiliations do not establish participant location. The arm-means/SDs/counts flag for fluency refers to reported means and SDs plus the overall sample counts; fluency-specific counts are not established. The only unresolved design classification is the RCT setting, not whether people were randomly assigned.
